title: Statistical Interpretation of Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics: The Underlying Explanation
lead: The other formulations of the second law of thermodynamics say what happens; this section says why. A macrostate is what you can see of a system, such as the number of heads in a toss of coins or the pressure and temperature of a gas, and a microstate is one detailed arrangement that produces it. Every microstate is equally probable, and the disorderly macrostates have vastly more microstates than the orderly ones, so a system left to itself goes from order to disorder because that is overwhelmingly the more likely outcome. Boltzmann's expression, the entropy as his constant times the natural logarithm of the number of microstates, ties the entropy of a macrostate to that count, and the change in entropy between two macrostates follows from their counts.
objectives: Analyze statistical probabilities in entropic systems.
summary_html:
• Disorder is far more likely than order, which can be seen statistically.
  • The entropy of a system in a given state (a macrostate) can be written as $$\kSent = k\ln W,$$ where $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}$ is Boltzmann’s constant, and $\ln W$ is the natural logarithm of the number of microstates $W$ corresponding to the given macrostate.
notes: Figure 15.37, the photograph of tossed coins at the head of the section, is left out as a splash image, and the four problems the book leaves unkeyed are left out: the percent of tosses from 60 heads through 40 heads, 100 coins tossed from 45 heads to 51 and to 75, the three most likely macrostates of 10 coins with the time it takes to toss 10 heads, and the air conditioner whose heat transfer is measured in melted ice; the book’s lowercase entropy s and the five microstates Table 15.3 prints twice in its 3-heads row are kept as printed.

figures.original_caption: (a) The ordinary state of gas in a container is a disorderly, random distribution of atoms or molecules with a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of speeds. It is so unlikely that these atoms or molecules would ever end up in one corner of the container that it might as well be impossible. (b) With energy transfer, the gas can be forced into one corner and its entropy greatly reduced. But left alone, it will spontaneously increase its entropy and return to the normal conditions, because they are immensely more likely.

exercises.prompt: Explain why a building made of bricks has smaller entropy than the same bricks in a disorganized pile. Do this by considering the number of ways that each could be formed (the number of microstates in each macrostate).

answer.solution: Take the bricks as the parts of the system and the two macrostates as the building and the pile. A building is a particular arrangement: each brick has a place it must occupy and a way it must face, and a brick out of place or turned the wrong way no longer makes that building, so there is essentially one way, or at most a handful of ways, to form it from the bricks. A disorganized pile is any arrangement at all: the bricks can lie in any order, at any angle and in any heap, and every one of those arrangements is still the same pile, so the number of microstates of the pile is enormous. The entropy of a macrostate is $\kSent = k\ln W$, where $W$ is the number of microstates that produce it, so the building, with its few microstates, has a much smaller entropy than the pile, which can be formed in an immense number of ways. This is also why a building can fall into a pile and a pile never gathers itself into a building: the pile is overwhelmingly the more probable macrostate, and the change from building to pile is an increase in entropy.

exercises.prompt: A piston is resting halfway into a cylinder containing gas in thermal equilibrium. The layer of molecules next to the closed end of the cylinder is suddenly flash-heated to a very high temperature. Which best describes what happens next?

options: The high temperature molecules push out the piston until their energy is reduced enough that the system is in equilibrium.
The molecules with the highest temperature bounce off their neighbors, losing energy to them, and so on until the system is at a new equilibrium with the piston moved out.
The molecules with the highest temperature bounce off their neighbors, losing energy to them, and so on until the system is at a new equilibrium with the piston where it started.
The high temperature molecules push out the piston until their energy is reduced enough that the system is in equilibrium, and then the piston gets sucked back in.
answer.hint: The flash-heated layer is far from the piston and holds its extra energy only until it collides with its neighbors. Think about how the energy spreads through the gas by collisions, and then about what a gas that is warmer than before does to a piston it is pushing against.

exercises.prompt: Design a macroscopic simulation using reasonably common materials to represent one very high energy particle gradually transferring energy to a bunch of lower energy particles, and determine if you end up with some sort of equilibrium.

answer.solution: One simple version uses a set of identical balls on a smooth, level surface, such as the balls on a billiard table or a bag of marbles on a tray. Spread most of them over the surface at rest, or rolling slowly in random directions, and send one ball in fast; that ball is the very high energy particle. It strikes a neighbor and shares its kinetic energy with it, as the collisions of Chapter 8 describe, the two of them strike others, and after a few rounds of collisions no ball is moving much faster than the rest. To decide whether an equilibrium has been reached, record the motion, for example by filming the surface and measuring how far each ball moves between frames, and see whether the spread of speeds settles to a steady pattern in which the ball that started fast can no longer be picked out; that steady spread of speeds in random directions is the macroscopic version of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of kinetic theory. The simulation is imperfect, because rolling friction removes energy that the atoms of a gas would keep, so the balls slow and stop; pucks on an air table come closer. Either way, the energy that began in one ball is never seen to gather back into one ball, because the arrangement in which it is shared among all of them has vastly more microstates than the arrangement in which one ball has it all, which is the reason the flash-heated layer of gas in the previous item spreads its energy and never regains it.

exercises.prompt: Using Table 15.4, verify the contention that if you toss 100 coins each second, you can expect to get 100 heads or 100 tails once in $2\times10^{22}$ years; calculate the time to two-digit accuracy.

answer.hint: Table 15.4 gives the total number of microstates of 100 coins, and all heads and all tails are one microstate each, so together they come up twice in every $1.27\times10^{30}$ tosses. At a toss a second, that count of tosses is a count of seconds, to be turned into years.
answer.solution: It should happen twice in every $1.27\times10^{30}\ \text{s}$ or once in every $6.35\times10^{29}\ \text{s}$. $(6.35\times10^{29}\ \text{s})\left(\frac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}}\right)\left(\frac{1\ \text{d}}{24\ \text{h}}\right)\left(\frac{1\ \text{y}}{365.25\ \text{d}}\right) = 2.0\times10^{22}\ \text{y}$

exercises.prompt: (a) If tossing 100 coins, how many ways (microstates) are there to get the three most likely macrostates of 49 heads and 51 tails, 50 heads and 50 tails, and 51 heads and 49 tails? (b) What percent of the total possibilities is this? (Consult Table 15.4.)

parts.hint: Read the number of microstates of each of the three macrostates from Table 15.4 and add them.
Divide the sum by the total number of microstates of 100 coins, $1.27\times10^{30}$, and write the fraction as a percent.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the change in entropy if you start with 10 coins in the 5 heads and 5 tails macrostate, toss them, and get 2 heads and 8 tails? (b) How much more likely is 5 heads and 5 tails than 2 heads and 8 tails? (Take the ratio of the number of microstates to find out.) (c) If you were betting on 2 heads and 8 tails would you accept odds of 252 to 45? Explain why or why not.

parts.hint: Table 15.5 gives $W = 252$ for 5 heads and 5 tails and $W = 45$ for 2 heads and 8 tails. The change is $\kdS = k\ln W_{\text{f}} - k\ln W_{\text{i}}$, and it is negative because the final macrostate is the more orderly one.
How much more likely one macrostate is than another is the ratio of their numbers of microstates.

answer.solution: (a) $-2.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}$ (b) 5.6 times more likely (c) If you were betting on two heads and 8 tails, the odds of breaking even are 252 to 45, so on average you would break even. So, no, you wouldn’t bet on odds of 252 to 45.

exercises.prompt: (a) Construct a table showing the macrostates and all of the individual microstates for tossing 6 coins. (Use Table 15.5 as a guide.) (b) How many macrostates are there? (c) What is the total number of microstates? (d) What percent chance is there of tossing 5 heads and 1 tail? (e) How much more likely are you to toss 3 heads and 3 tails than 5 heads and 1 tail? (Take the ratio of the number of microstates to find out.)

parts.hint: With 6 coins the number of heads runs from 0 to 6, and each count is one macrostate.
Each coin has two faces, so the total number of sequences is 2 multiplied by itself six times.
Count the sequences with exactly one tail, which can be any one of the six coins, and divide by the total number of microstates.
Take the ratio of the number of microstates of 3 heads and 3 tails to the number for 5 heads and 1 tail.
